content: Epidemiological studies and meta-analyses of predictive research consistently highlight the critical role of psychosocial and psychological factors as risk contributors to postpartum depression. While interventions targeting these factors are effective treatment strategies, they may also serve as preventive measures during pregnancy and the early postpartum period. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of various psychosocial and psychological interventions compared to standard antenatal, intrapartum, or postpartum care in reducing the risk of postpartum depression. Secondary objectives included assessing the effectiveness of specific types of interventions, comparing professionally-delivered versus lay-delivered interventions, evaluating individual-based versus group-based approaches, analyzing the effects of intervention timing and duration, and determining whether interventions are more effective in women identified with specific risk factors. The review included a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register up to November 30, 2011, with an update on December 31, 2012. Both published and unpublished randomized controlled trials of acceptable quality were included, comparing psychosocial or psychological interventions with usual care. Methodological quality and data extraction were assessed by experienced reviewers, and additional information was obtained from trial researchers. Results were presented using risk ratios (RR) for categorical data and mean differences (MD) for continuous data. Data from 28 trials involving nearly 17,000 women were analyzed. Women who received psychosocial or psychological interventions were significantly less likely to develop postpartum depression compared to those receiving standard care (average RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.93; 20 trials, 14,727 women). Several interventions showed particular promise: 1. Intensive, individualized postpartum home visits conducted by public health nurses or midwives significantly reduced the risk of postpartum depression (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.73; two trials, 1,262 women). 2. Telephone-based peer support was highly effective (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.77; one trial, 612 women). 3. Interpersonal psychotherapy demonstrated a significant reduction in depressive symptoms (standardized mean difference -0.27, 95% CI -0.52 to -0.01; five trials, 366 women). Both professionally-delivered and lay-delivered interventions were effective in reducing the risk of developing depressive symptoms. Individually-based interventions were particularly beneficial, reducing depressive symptoms at the final assessment (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.92; 14 trials, 12,914 women). Similarly, interventions involving multiple contacts were effective (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.93; 16 trials, 11,850 women). Interventions initiated during the postpartum period also significantly reduced the risk of depressive symptoms (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90; 12 trials, 12,786 women). Targeting women identified as at-risk for postpartum depression further enhanced the effectiveness of preventive measures (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88; eight trials, 1,853 women). In conclusion, psychosocial and psychological interventions significantly reduce the incidence of postpartum depression. Promising strategies include intensive, professionally-delivered postpartum home visits, telephone-based peer support, and interpersonal psychotherapy. These findings underscore the importance of implementing targeted, evidence-based interventions to prevent postpartum depression, particularly in at-risk populations.
